feedback: If a learner routes air to the stomach, re-trace the airway path trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli, and emphasise the thin alveolar wall where oxygen diffuses into capillaries.
If a learner answers that the lungs pull the air, restate the pressure mechanism: enlarging the chest lowers pressure; outside air is pushed in.
A labelled diagram names and locates structures but does not by itself show the pressure mechanism — pair it with the model activity so the mechanism is seen in action.
activities.intendedInsight: The gas exchange system has a named, ordered structure, and air enters the blood specifically at the alveoli — pushed by pressure, not pulled by the lungs.
learnerActions: Label a lung/airway diagram: trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Trace the path of a single inhaled oxygen molecule from the trachea to the moment it crosses into the blood at an alveolus.
Answer the question 'Do the lungs suck air in?' and give the correct reason: no — the diaphragm enlarges the chest, pressure drops, and air is pushed in.
Attach each alveolar adaptation to its benefit (thin wall + big surface + good blood supply = fast diffusion).
activities.title: Name the airway structures and bust the 'lungs suck' myth

feedback: If a learner says exhaled air is pure CO₂, give the real figures: inhaled air is about 21% oxygen, exhaled about 16% — only a few percent less. Only SOME oxygen diffuses into the blood; exhaled air is still mostly nitrogen with plenty of oxygen, which is exactly why rescue breaths can work.

If a learner conflates breathing and respiration, restate: breathing is the pressure-driven movement of air; respiration is energy release inside cells; gas exchange is diffusion at the alveoli that links them.
If the inhalation order is wrong, re-anchor on cause and effect: muscle contraction must come before volume change, which comes before pressure change, which comes before airflow.
activities.intendedInsight: Breathing, gas exchange and respiration are three distinct processes; sequencing the breathing events and separating the three ideas confirms the learner is not conflating them.
learnerActions: Put the events of inhalation in order (e.g. diaphragm contracts and flattens while the external intercostal muscles contract to lift the ribs up and out → chest volume increases → pressure falls → air moves in).
Match each alveolar adaptation to how it helps diffusion.
Sort or classify statements into breathing (ventilation), gas exchange (diffusion at the alveoli), and respiration (energy release in cells), explaining what distinguishes each.
Decide whether exhaled air is pure carbon dioxide or still contains oxygen, and justify the answer.
Explain the full breathing mechanism in your own words to show the chain is understood, not just recognised.
activities.title: Check and separate breathing, gas exchange and respiration
